definition: Forestall means to prevent something by acting ahead of time.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word forestall. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know forestall should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Knowing the twins would fight over the last slice, their mother forestalled the argument by cutting it in two before dinner.
Containing a problem is weaker than forestalling it — the trouble has already begun, and you are only limiting its spread.
Averting is a step short of forestalling — a disaster can be averted at the last instant, while forestalling means you moved long before the danger was even close.

To preempt is to act first so that another's move never happens or no longer matters — it needs a rival plan to beat. To forestall needs no rival: you see any kind of trouble coming and act early enough that it never starts.

To preclude is to shut a possibility off in advance — the rule, the design, or the circumstance makes the thing impossible, no foresight story required. To forestall is personal and tactical: someone reads what is coming and moves early to stop it.

The festival's planners forestalled the annual parking chaos by chartering shuttle buses a month in advance and selling lot passes with every ticket.
Any barrier can prevent; forestall specifically means getting ahead of the problem.
The timing is the point — you see what is coming and act early enough that it never gets started at all.
Forestall is the strategist's word: it praises foresight, not reflexes.
Use 'prevent' when timing doesn't matter and 'avert' for the last-second save; reach for forestall when someone read the future and moved early.
Unlike its unit-mates quell and neutralize, which deal with trouble already alive, forestall wins by making sure the trouble is never born.

Frost does its worst work in the last hour before dawn, and by then it is far too late to fight.
So the orchardists of the valley learned to read the afternoon instead: a hard blue sky, a wind that dies at dusk, a thermometer falling fast by nine.
On those nights they light the smudge pots at midnight to forestall the freeze, stirring the cold air before it can settle into the blossoms.
Neighbors who wait for the first white on the grass lose their crop; the ones who act on the afternoon's warnings keep theirs.
The whole trick, one grower says, is doing the work while there is still nothing to see.
